outline: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
mechanism: Abnormal separation of the embryonic esophagus and trachea from their common foregut precursor produces esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula; a distal fistula allows air from the airway to enter the stomach.
vignette: A newborn develops coughing, cyanosis, and copious oral secretions with the first feeding. An orogastric tube cannot be advanced into the stomach. Radiography shows the tube terminating in the upper esophagus and air within the stomach.
lead: Which embryologic abnormality most likely caused this condition?
correct: Failure of tracheoesophageal separation of the primitive foregut
distractors: Failure of enteric neural crest migration to the distal colon
Failure of the herniated midgut to return to the abdominal cavity
distractor_notes: Failed duodenal recanalization causes duodenal atresia; it does not explain a tube terminating in the upper esophagus.
Abnormal enteric neural crest migration/differentiation causes Hirschsprung disease with distal bowel aganglionosis, not esophageal discontinuity.
Failure of herniated bowel to return to the abdominal cavity produces omphalocele, an abdominal-wall defect rather than esophageal atresia.
Persistent vitelline duct causes vitelline-duct remnants such as a vitelline fistula or Meckel diverticulum, not esophageal atresia.
key_expl: The feeding-associated cough/cyanosis plus failure of an orogastric tube to reach the stomach identifies esophageal atresia. Air in the stomach supports a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. EA/TEF results when the embryonic esophagus and trachea fail to separate normally from their common foregut precursor.
objective: Recognize esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula from neonatal feeding-related respiratory symptoms and failed gastric-tube passage, and relate the defect to abnormal tracheoesophageal separation.
clues: orogastric tube stops in upper esophagus
air in stomach despite esophageal atresia

sources.organization: CDC, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities
sources.title: Esophageal Atresia
sources.locator: What it is; Types — Type C; Diagnosis
sources.support: CDC states that esophageal atresia creates disconnected upper and lower esophageal segments, commonly occurs with tracheoesophageal fistula, Type C has a closed upper segment with the lower segment attached to the trachea, and diagnosis is suggested when feeding causes choking/vomiting and a tube cannot pass into the stomach.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus Genetics
sources.title: Esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that the embryonic esophagus and trachea begin as a single tube that normally divides into two passages and that improper separation results in EA/TEF; it also describes feeding-related cough, respiratory distress/cyanosis, and distal TEF as the common configuration.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Embryology, Gastrointestinal
sources.support: NCBI describes esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula allowing air to enter the stomach and separately identifies failed duodenal recanalization, abnormal enteric neural crest development, failure of bowel return in omphalocele, and persistence of the vitelline duct as mechanisms of the distractor conditions.
